Think of quantization like the difference between a 4K cinematic trailer and a compressed 720p stream. When AI developers train a massive model, they usually save it in high-precision formats—essentially 4K video files for math. Every single connection in that neural network is stored with extreme detail, using 16-bit or even 32-bit numbers. That sounds precise, but it also means the file is enormous, and your GPU has to crunch through a lot of data to run it. For a gamer buying their first card, that is usually a dealbreaker. You might have a decent RTX 4070 or 4080, but loading a 70-billion-parameter model in full precision could require 140 gigabytes of VRAM—more than your entire system has.

Quantization is the process of squeezing that high-definition file down without losing the plot. Instead of storing every weight with perfect precision, you round them to simpler values, often reducing them to 8-bit or even 4-bit integers. It is like telling your GPU, "You don’t need to know the exact shade of every pixel; just tell me if it’s dark or light." The model still understands language, generates images, or plays games, but it does so with far less memory and often faster inference speeds because the math is simpler. For your first GPU, this is the difference between being able to run a useful AI assistant and staring at an "out of memory" error.

When you download a massive AI model, it’s essentially a giant brain made of billions of tiny numbers—weights—that tell it how to think. By default, those numbers are stored in high precision, usually 16-bit or 32-bit, which is like saving every pixel in perfect, uncompressed detail. That sounds great, but it makes the file enormous and demands a GPU with a mountain of VRAM, often costing thousands of dollars. Quantization is the process of squeezing those numbers down, usually to 8-bit or even 4-bit, so they take up far less space and run faster on your card.

For a gamer, this is the secret sauce that lets you run LLMs on a $500 or $800 GPU instead of a $3,000 workstation. Imagine you have a 7-billion parameter model. In full precision, it might need 14GB of VRAM just to load. Quantized to 4-bit, it might only need 4GB. That’s the difference between needing an RTX 4090 and being able to run it comfortably on an RTX 4070 or even a used 3090. The trade-off is quality, but for most local AI tasks—chatting, summarizing text, or coding assistance—the drop is surprisingly small. It’s like turning down the graphics settings from "Ultra" to "High": you might miss some subtle background details, but the gameplay is still smooth and the story is still clear.

There are different flavors of this compression. You’ll see terms like GGUF, AWQ, or GPTQ. Don’t let the acronyms scare you; they’re just different recipes for the same idea. GGUF is popular for local runners like Ollama or LM Studio because it’s flexible and works well across different hardware. AWQ and GPTQ are often used in more specialized setups. The key thing to remember is that quantization isn’t just about file size; it’s about speed. Lower precision means your GPU’s memory bandwidth isn’t choked by moving massive amounts of data, so tokens generate faster. For a first-time buyer, this means you can prioritize VRAM capacity and memory bandwidth over raw compute power, because a quantized model will run happily on a card that wouldn’t touch the full-precision version.

import asyncio
import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Any, Callable, Generic, Hashable, Optional, TypeVar

class AsyncLRUCache(Generic[T]):
    """A thread-safe (asyncio-safe) LRU cache with per-entry TTL.

    This cache uses an ``OrderedDict`` to maintain insertion/access order
    and an ``asyncio.Lock`` to ensure that concurrent coroutines do not
    corrupt the internal state. Each entry can have its own time-to-live
    (TTL) in seconds; expired entries are evicted lazily upon access.

    Attributes:
        max_size: Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
        default_ttl: Default TTL (seconds) applied when ``ttl`` is not
            specified in :meth:`put`.
    """

    def __init__(self, max_size: int = 128, default_ttl: float = 0.0) -> None:
        """Initialize the cache.

        Args:
            max_size: Maximum number of items to store. Must be > 0.
            default_ttl: Default time-to-live in seconds. A value of 0.0
                means entries never expire by default.
        """

            raise ValueError("max_size must be positive")

        self._default_ttl: float = default_ttl

"""An asyncio-safe LRU cache with per-entry TTL support."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import time
from collections import OrderedDict
from typing import Any, Callable, Generic, Hashable, Optional, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


class AsyncLRUCache(Generic[T]):
    """A thread-safe (asyncio-safe) LRU cache with per-entry TTL.

    This cache uses an ``OrderedDict`` to maintain insertion/access order
    and an ``asyncio.Lock`` to ensure that concurrent coroutines do not
    corrupt the internal state. Each entry can have its own time-to-live
    (TTL) in seconds; expired entries are evicted lazily upon access.

    Attributes:
        max_size: Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
        default_ttl: Default TTL (seconds) applied when ``ttl`` is not
            specified in :meth:`put`.
    """

    def __init__(self, max_size: int, default_ttl: float = 0.0) -> None:
        """Initialize the cache.

        Args:
            max_size: Maximum number of items to store. Must be > 0.
            default_ttl: Default time-to-live in seconds. A value of 0.0
                means entries never expire by default.
        """
        if max_size <= 0:
            raise ValueError("max_size must be positive")
        self._max_size: int = max_size
        self._default_ttl: float = default_ttl
        self._data: OrderedDict[Hashable, tuple[T, float, float]] = OrderedDict()
        self._lock: asyncio.Lock = asyncio.Lock()

    @property
    def max_size(self) -> int:
        """Return the maximum capacity of the cache."""
        return self._max_size

    @property
    def default_ttl(self) -> float:
        """Return the default TTL in seconds."""
        return self._default_ttl

    def _is_expired(self, expires_at: float) -> bool:
        """Check whether an entry has expired.

        Args:
            expires_at: The absolute timestamp (seconds since epoch) at
                which the entry expires.

        Returns:
            True if the entry is expired, False otherwise.
        """
        return expires_at > 0.0 and time.monotonic()
